items.title: Final Fantasy producer "very happy" Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 took inspiration from Square Enix's JRPGs, because he was just as inspired by Star Wars
items.content:
JRPGs Final Fantasy Final Fantasy X / X-2 HD Remaster Final Fantasy producer "very happy" Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 took inspiration from Square Enix's JRPGs, because he was just as inspired by Star Wars News By Scott McCrae Published 5 November 2026 Final Fantasy 10's Blitzball was based on The Phantom Menace's Pod Racing

(Image credit: Square Enix) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 0 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Final Fantasy series producer Yoshinori Kitase says that Final Fantasy 10 's iconic Blitzball minigame was inspired in-part by Pod Racing in Star Wars Episode 1: The Phantom Menace – so he's pleased that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 took inspiration from Square Enix 's series, too.

Kitase – who served as game director of Final Fantasy 10 – spoke to IGN about being "very happy" that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 was so inspired by Final Fantasy because he himself was inspired by movies he enjoyed when he was young – particularly Star Wars.

"I think I like Star Wars so much that I was afraid of using anything related to [it]," Kitase says, recalling the fear that his work would become something identical to the films. He explains, "I don't think there's something from the movie that I used directly as an inspiration for my games."

However, he does admit to a couple of major inspirations, namely Biggs and Wedge – recurring names used in the series starting with Final Fantasy 6 – who are named after Luke Skywalker's wingmen during the attack on the Death Star in the original Star Wars (Biggs Darklighter and Wedge Antilles). He recalls, "I wasn't sure about the name I was going to use for those characters. And I ended up using the names of characters from Star Wars."

Another major inspiration came when Kitase was creating the fictional sport Blitzball for inclusion in the game. He recalls, "I used an idea from Star Wars Episode 1 where there's this [pod] race and the fact of using sport inside a fantasy context, I took this idea directly from Star Wars."

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is set after ROTJ because it mirrors the post-WW2 motorsports boom After countless memes, Final Fantasy 7 Revelation boss confirms that, yes, Fortnite inspired jumping out of the Highwind Square Enix's "graphical goal" for Final Fantasy 7 remakes was 2005 spin-off film Advent Children Frankly, I'm more impressed that he was able to be inspired by a film that released two years earlier, which is a massive reminder of how much quicker sequels to games released, and how on fire Square Enix was at that point. Kitase directed Final Fantasy 8 which released three months before The Phantom Menace, and two years later Final Fantasy 10 – inspired by The Phantom Menace – arrived on shelves.

Final Fantasy 10 leaned into the fantasy genre after devs "learned that The Lord of the Rings was in production" and thought it would be "the next big global trend."

He has also written for the likes of PC Gamer, Eurogamer, VG247, Play, TechRadar, and others. items.title: 10 Best Turn-Based RPG Masterpieces of the Last 20 Years
items.summary: RPGs like Baldur's Gate 3 show how addictive turn-based combat systems can be.
items.content:
Add CBR on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover By Sage Ashford Published Nov 3, 2026, 7:30 PM EST Staff Writer for CBR, Sage Ashford has also written for Comicon as well as other sites such as The Gamer, and has been doing freelance work since 2014, and been working for CBR since 2016. His focus is primarily on spreading the word on obscure anime, comic books, and games whenever possible. Follow him on Twitter @ sageshinigami, or on YouTube @ nolevelcap. Sign in to your CBR account Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Listen Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap While many people assume that turn-based RPGs are a relic of the past, the genre has thrived in the 21st century, and new games like Baldur's Gate 3 and Like a Dragon have built on the genre in fascinating ways. These titles have proven that turn-based combat can still be as challenging as involving as the battle systems in any action RPGs.

There have been many amazing turn-based RPGs released across the last 20 years, but these titles are the cream of the crop, and everyone who enjoys the genre should try to play them at least once. Not only do they have excellent gameplay, but they have intelligently written stories that place them in the running for some of the greatest RPGs ever made.

XCOM 2 gameplay screenshot showing a character in a giant mech suit getting ready to use a large alien cannon Image via Firaxis Games Firaxis Games already had their hands full trying to revive a franchise like XCOM , and after they succeeded they had to outdo themselves. Fortunately, fans generally regard XCOM 2 as not just a great game, but one of the best turn-based titles of the 2010s. Set decades after the first title, XCOM 2 shows humanity struggling to hold on after losing a war against an alien race, raising the stakes higher than ever.

XCOM 2 forces players to deal with the unpredictability of war, offering procedural generation for their maps, and making many of the game's upgrades happen in a nonlinear fashion. While some turn-based games can often feel too easy, XCOM 2 forces players to think about every move, and a few wrong decisions can ruin an entire mission. The result is one of the coolest tactical turn-based RPGs ever.

Rip Mystery Packs of Graded Cards & Collectibles

Japanese Pokémon Center 20th Anniversary Promo · PSA 10

Must be 18+/19+ to participate depending on jurisdiction.

Ochette, Castti, Throne, Osvald, Partitio, Agnea, Hikari, and Temenos at a camp in a forest in Octopath Traveler II Image via Square-Enix Square Enix's creation of HD-2D has been popular but had a mixed reception. Still, one game that hasn't had that problem is Octopath Traveler II . Much like the original, Octopath II sees players collecting eight separate travelers, each going on their own adventure. However, both the writing and the presentation take a noticeable jump, turning the game from merely "good" into "legendary".

With eight different "lead" protagonists, Octopath II offers a number of wildly varying stories, from Hikari's attempt to reclaim his stolen throne, to Agnea's desire to become a legendary dancer. The game's world is fleshed out enough for all these stories to fit together. With a well-developed class system and innovative turn-based combat, Octopath Traveler II will speak to anyone that loves unique combat systems and SNES-era vibes.

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

Wasteland 3 combat screenshot showing a giant mechanical vehicle attacking a city with a blast of energy Image via InExile Entertainment The original Wasteland helped inspire one of the most popular franchises of all time in Fallout . However, it remained dormant afterward until InXile came along, reviving the franchise and creating some fantastic games in the process. While people might think they know what they're in for with Wasteland 3 's post-apocalyptic setting, they'll find a completely different experience once they actually sit down and try it.

Wasteland 3 might offer some familiar tropes, but they're backed by some surprisingly great execution to make things feel fresh. In both main and side quests, every choice the player makes has ramifications they'll see later, helping to personalize their story, as few are going to always make the same choices. Meanwhile, the combat is frantic and challenging, forcing players to constantly adjust on the fly.

Dragon Quest XI main party including the Hero, Erik, Veronica, Serena, Sylvando, and Rab together Image via Square-Enix Dragon Quest XI: Echoes of an Elusive Age reminds players there's a reason all the best franchises have such staying power. While Dragon Quest isn't trying to reinvent the wheel, there's something to be said for creating a classic-styled JRPG that's smartly written. As the nameless Hero, players will learn to accept their role as the Luminary, someone destined to save the world.

The greatest turn-based RPGs of all time include masterpieces like Persona 5 and Final Fantasy X.

items.title: Is Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 not indie "just because someone helped with marketing?" Palworld lead says the definition of an indie studio has become "so blurred"
items.summary: Stardew Valley is in the same bracket
items.content:

(Image credit: Kepler Interactive) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 1 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter There are some blurred lines in the industry around what counts as indie or AAA nowadays. Is it about funding? Or scale? It's a discussion that frequently ripples up, and now someone involved in Palworld has weighed in.

John 'Bucky' Buckley, the head of publishing and communications at Palworld studio Pocketpair, gives his two cents on Twitter , going into how the economics have become "so blurred." He points out, for instance, that Palworld is fully self-funded. Pocketpair has no outside financial influence. Hence, the company believes it is indie by nearly any definition.

But where is the line if someone is taking outside money – often a necessity to get the project off the ground to begin with? "For me, creative independence is probably the most important factor. If a studio has genuine creative freedom, then I think it’s fair to consider them independent," he writes.

A pretty interesting write-up about how the label “indie” has become so blurred in recent years. We consider ourselves indie because we have zero outside investment or backing. Palworld and Pocketpair are entirely self-funded, but it’s understandable that our success makes people see us differently. On the flip side, many studios considered “indie”, including some that have won major awards and achieved huge success, have received funding and backing from much larger companies. So where does the indie line begin and end? …comments will quickly say “if you’re over X people then you aren’t Indie” but, I don’t think it can be clearly defined anymore. For me, creative independence is probably the most important factor. If a studio has genuine creative freedom, then I think it’s fair to consider them independent. If another entity is exerting creative pressure or making decisions for a studio, then I think that independence becomes questionable. Even then, plenty of studios receive external funding while retaining complete creative control. I don’t think having a publisher or investor automatically makes a studio any less indie. So yes, we still call ourselves indie. I know many people will disagree, and some will point to our size or the amount of money Palworld has made as reasons why we shouldn’t use that label. But from our pov, we’re 100% self-owned, we have no outside investors to answer to, and we have complete freedom to make the games we want to make. That’s what being indie means to us. If you’d rather call us iii or AA, that’s fine too! Ultimately, it’s just a label and all that really matters is that we’re still making fun games. October 29, 2026

"If another entity is exerting creative pressure or making decisions for a studio, then I think that independence becomes questionable," he adds. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 comes up in the replies, because the release that courted some discourse after being nominated for Best Indie Game at The Game Awards despite the devs using an outside publisher.

Buckley points out, though, that if the assistance is purely on the marketing side, is it fair to force the AAA distinction? "Is it really fair to say E33 isn't indie just because someone helped with marketing?" he asks, before pointing to another big example: "Can we really say 'Stardew [Valley] isn't indie because Chucklefish helped out with some marketing years ago?' I think there's a lot of nuance to the label now."

Palworld lead worries Steam early access "lost its meaning," players treat it as "a normal game" Palworld isn't following Fortnite because making money "as quickly as possible" isn't the mission Palworld lead tells fans they "simply do not realize the sheer number of collabs we've rejected" Stardew is a huge franchise by now, with an official tour for the soundtrack, and yet the core game is still handled by ConcernedApe and a small team. It varies by degrees, but in Buckley's mind, it comes down to one abiding principle.

"Creative control is king," Buckley states. It's hard to argue, even if it's also sometimes hard to distinguish the team's dynamic from the outset.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Nintendo might be suing them, but Palworld CEO would still "love" to talk about bringing the survival game to Switch 2.

items.title: Game Pass Is About To Lose Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 And Some Other Incredible Games
items.summary: The RPG sensation and more gems are leaving in October
items.content:
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 was one of 2025’s best games and one of the best third-party releases ever to join Game Pass day-and-date. Players have now had over a year to finish the turn-based RPG, but for any subscribers who haven’t yet taken the plunge, time is running out. The GOTY winner is leaving Game Pass on October 15.

That leaves you just under two weeks to go and complete the journey or start it from scratch. You can rush the main story to clear it in under 30 hours, but if you want to mine all of the expanded content, a completionist run will take you more than twice that. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is one of the rare JRPG-inspired games that’s managed to break through in the modern era to a broader audience, in part thanks to its novel dodge and parry mechanics which inject some fresh energy into the usual turn-based grind. It’s also worth making it all the way through to hit the twist ending .

But Clair Obscur is also not the only great game leaving Game Pass this month . The full list includes:

Pacific Drive and A Plague Tale Requiem are both excellent, especially for the spooky month. The former is a sci-fi survival crafting game about navigating a zone full of strange anomalies with a haunted station wagon. The latter is about surviving a late medieval Europe infested with disease carrying rats. Donut County , on the other hand, is a light hearted puzzle game you can finish in just a few hours that is still one of my favorite indie games of all time.

Expeditioners!

Following the huge demand from so many of you, we’ve been working super hard to be able to finally announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, is now available with Arabic text!

This brings the total number of supported languages to 20!

With the new Arabic language support, we had to consider additional changes to the game’s UI to ensure a smooth and enjoyable experience for Arabic-speaking players around the world.

Adding Arabic localization has been a true team effort over many months, from the incredible adaptation and localization work carried out by the linguists, to reworking the vast majority of the user interface for right-to-left reading, all the way through localization testing.

Every team involved brought passion and dedication to making this possible, and we couldn’t be more grateful for their work. We hope this update makes the story feel even more personal to our players.

Today’s update also includes some additional fixes and improvements. Read the full patch notes here!

Thank you all so much for your continued support! <3

Tomorrow comes.

~ The Expedition 33 Team

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is '95 percent' made with Blueprints
items.summary: Sticking to a nearly-vanilla version of Unreal Engine kept Sandfall Interactive on track.
items.content:
Keep up with the latest news, interviews, talk coverage, and other game dev insights from GDC right here on Game Developer. Read More

Sticking to a nearly-vanilla version of Unreal Engine kept Sandfall Interactive on track.

Much has been made of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 developer Sandfall Interactive's production process. As you've probably heard by now, the smash hit game was produced by a studio that employs fewer than 40 people, and everyone in the game industry has a hot take about what made that possible (and often ignore the hundreds of other people listed in the game's credits ).

They've been so prolific that at a GDC Festival of Gaming talk from Sandfall chief technical officer Tom Guillermin and senior gameplay programmer Florian Torres had an entire slide advising the audience not to use their presentation as a roadmap. "This is not meant to be a tutorial or like a how-to guide on how to make games," said Guillermin. "It's a retrospective on how we made Expedition 33 ."

But let's face it, when your studio's first game is such a highly-polished hit, everyone will obviously be trying to copy your homework. Developers aiming to learn about Sandfal's process swarmed Moscone West, and let out a collective murmur of shock when Guillermin and Torres described how their small team of programmers supported such an expensive-looking game—they just used a near-vanilla version of Unreal Engine.

Related: Clair Obscur writer shares production advice that could improve your game's story

And they didn't use Unreal Engine to write lines and lines and lines of code in C++. Expedition 33 was largely made with Unreal's Blueprints system.

According to Torres, 95 percent of the game was constructed in Blueprints.

For the uninitiated, Unreal Engine's Blueprints system is a visual scripting tool that lets developers link "nodes" together to create different gameplay elements. It's used to define object-oriented objects or classes in the game engine. For laypeople, this mean it lets developers assemble game logic by stringing together nodes of scripting logic without constantly coding in C++.

On Clair Obscur , this meant that Guillermin, Torres, and the rest of the programmers could hand off content and feature development to the studio's designers and artists, allowing them to produce and test content in the game engine with fewer roadblocks that would rely on a programmer to create code.

Unreal Engine developers use Blueprints to different degrees. The system is deeply tied into Unreal Engine's natural codebase, and if you need to modify the engine in any way, the system becomes less reliable. In fact Guillermin said that Sandfall has a very "vanilla-first" approach when it comes to using Unreal. "We take all the tools that are natively present and we push them to their to their limits so we don't have to develop bespoke tools for the features and content of the of the game," he said.

Related: Anthropic orders AI tool Claude to stop remaking video games

Photo via the author, slide by Sandfall Interactive

The only "modifications" they used were old-fashioned Unreal plugins like CommonUI, GeometryScripting, ALS (Advanced Locomotion System) and KawaiiPhysics (which one commentator on Bluesky described as "one guy's freeware project for doing swooshy anime hair physics.")

items.summary: Introducing a special bundle featuring the award‑winning fantasy RPG “Metaphor: ReFantazio”, created by the team behind Persona 3-5, paired with “Clair Obscur: Expedition 33” - now available at 10% off! Enjoy both titles and experience the
items.content:
Introducing a special bundle featuring the award‑winning fantasy RPG “Metaphor: ReFantazio”, created by the team behind Persona 3-5, paired with “Clair Obscur: Expedition 33” - now available at 10% off!

Enjoy both titles and experience the worlds for yourself!

The Metaphor: ReFantazio × Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Bundle includes two games: “Metaphor: ReFantazio” and “Clair Obscur: Expedition 33.”

Message from Guillaume Broche & Katsura Hashino

"Metaphor: ReFantazio is a game that is really inspiring for us. It tells a beautiful story in a completely new world that is masterfully crafted. It deals with heavy themes but one that resonates strongly with me is the importance of imagination in all aspects of our lives. The cast is lovable and the turn-based battle system is one of the best I have played. The re-imagination of the traditional jobs system through Archetypes is fantastic and opens up so many playstyles that are fun to play around with. On top of that, the game has one of the most charismatic villains I've ever seen in an RPG. It is a great honor to be able to collaborate with Atlus on this bundle, as I have been a fan of their work since Shin Megami Tensei: Lucifer's Call (also known as Shin Megami Tensei III Nocturne for some players)." - Guillaume Broche

"I am Katsura Hashino from ATLUS, serving as the Creative Director for “Metaphor: ReFantazio.” I am very pleased to hear that a Steam bundle will be released with “Expedition 33,” a title that has received high praise around the world.

“Expedition 33” is a work that conveys a deep understanding of and sincere dedication to the JRPG genre, crafted with great care down to the finest details. As someone who also creates RPGs, I found it to be truly inspiring.

I am genuinely delighted to see Japanese-style RPGs being born and embraced, not only from Japanese-based studios like ours, but other places around the world through diverse creative approaches.

While the two titles differ in their worlds and overall direction, players may find a shared spirit in how we each approach and express the RPG genre. I hope that this bundle encourages players to experience both titles and enjoy the breadth of what RPGs can offer."

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 | Dev Blog - Photo Mode
items.summary: Expeditioners, We're so pleased to see so many of you enjoying the new photo mode feature!! We put a lot of time and care into building this feature and we’re so glad to see so many of you enjoying it! There were a lot of moving parts invol
items.content:
Expeditioners,

We're so pleased to see so many of you enjoying the new photo mode feature!!

We put a lot of time and care into building this feature and we’re so glad to see so many of you enjoying it! There were a lot of moving parts involved in getting the Photo Mode set up, so we thought we’d show a bit of the process in this blog and talk a bit about what went into building this feature.

There were a few key people involved in the development of this, and each of them had a part to write here !

VINCENT CONSTANTIN-TURKI – Producer \

One of the main features we wanted to introduce with the Thank You Update was Photo Mode. It felt like a meaningful way to give something back to the players and thank them for their commitment to the game.

What’s funny is that the team in charge of developing Photo Mode doesn’t usually use this feature in other games, which is why we decided to collaborate with Shinobi. He helped us design a Photo Mode that would truly resonate with players.

NAJA DALMAGNE – QA Coordinator \

In many games we tested, Photo Modes often felt restrictive, which could quickly become frustrating. So, from the very beginning, one of the key goals we all agreed on was to give players as much freedom as possible. It was really about letting players express their creativity without getting in the way.

During development, the QA team ran into some unexpected and sometimes quite funny issues. One of the funniest, but also one of the most severe, involved characters whose heads or torsos could become displaced or deformed when opening the Photo Mode if they hadn’t been visible on screen for a while during exploration.

One feature I’m particularly proud of is the lighting system Florian worked on. It offers great flexibility while remaining fairly easy to use, which really makes a difference when you're trying to get the perfect shot.

FLORIAN TORRES – Senior Gameplay Programmer \ \

I love giving players as many tools and features as possible (that’s literally the purpose of my job).

When we started working on the photo mode, our goal was to give players as few restrictions as possible and that’s what I was in charge of coding: infinite camera distance, the ability to pass through collisions, lots of customizable lights, many (weird) filters, and more.

Of course, that comes with its challenges, but in the end it allows players to see a lot of things we don’t want to show during normal gameplay. The photo mode became a way to peek behind the scenes of each cinematic or environment, and sometimes even see how we have created the entire game.

Ever wondered what happens outside the camera frame? Here’s an example (sorry cinematic team, I love you).

LUDOVIC ‘SHINOBI’ HELME – Photo Mode Consultant \

We felt it was important to include anything that increases the “freedom” factor for players. It opens up countless possibilities every time someone enters photo mode: a very generous camera range to capture unseen details or create epic compositions, RGB curves control to edit and build your own color schemes, a strong custom lighting system to truly take ownership of a scene, and solid depth-of-field management.

But when all of that is also available in cutscenes - giving access to those incredible facial expressions and emotions - that’s when I really start to feel satisfied.

Every shot I’ve seen has blown my mind, and I often wish I’d been the one to come up with the idea. It’s truly inspiring.

I’m very proud that the team managed to create a tool that is both beginner-friendly and deeply satisfying for more experienced photographers. Finding that balance is extremely difficult.

With all of these features, there had to be a user-friendly way for people to make use of everything. Making sure players had full control of all the settings and could navigate all the features comes down to our awesome Gameplay & UI Programmer, VICTOR BOULEZ.

Thank you for all of your appreciation and feedback on this feature, we had a lot of fun making it and even more fun watching you use it!

This past week, especially, we’ve really loved the work you’ve all been putting into the social Photo Mode Prompt Challenge!! We’ve seen some amazing photography this past week, it’s completely blown our minds how creative you have been able to get with the prompts and tools.

Even though the challenge is over, feel free to keep sharing your work with us on social media, we thoroughly enjoy seeing some of your masterpieces!!

In the meantime, we are continuing to work on fixes for ongoing problems, keep an eye on the bug thread and socials to stay updated on the latest.

Finally, we leave you with some of our favourite uses of photo mode.

items.title: I played Cory in the House for Nintendo DS to find out if it’s truly better than Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
items.summary: I played the Disney game threatening Clair Obscur: Expedition 33’s top Metacritic ranking — is it actually good?
items.content:
When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works .

(Image credit: Future / Nintendo / Disney / Sandfall Interactive / Kepler Interactive) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Threads Email Share this article 9 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Cory in the House for the Nintendo DS. That’s a name I haven’t heard in a long time. See, this 2008-released ‘adventure stealth’ game – as well as the TV show it’s based on – has been a meme for more than a decade. In the past, I’d often see Cory in the House being described as the ‘best anime of all time’. I’d also read Amazon reviews of the video game, which would hail it as a true ‘masterpiece’.

And now, in 2026, the meme seems to have been reborn. Users have taken to Metacritic and flooded it with positive reviews for Cory in the House on the Nintendo DS. And now, its user score sits at 9.3, which is indicative of ‘universal acclaim’. That score is so high, in fact, that the title is genuinely posing a threat to the top-ranked game on Metacritic by user score. And that game is none other than TechRadar’s Game of the Year of 2025, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 .

After hearing all of this, you may be wondering: is Cory in the House on Nintendo DS actually good? Well, it’s your lucky day. See, back in my teens, a friend of mine jokingly gifted me the game for Christmas, and thankfully, I still own it to this day. So, I dusted the cartridge off, put it in my Nintendo 3DS console, and played through it for the very first time. Here’s what I made of my time with the ‘universally acclaimed’ title.

My game card didn’t work at first, but after a few blows and re-insertions, I was finally in. When I reached the main menu, there were a few options to choose from, including Story, an arcade mode, and a gallery. I got straight into the Story mode, and well…it was quite something.

In this campaign, you play as Cory Baxter, a teenager whose dad works as the head chef at The White House. As an aspiring businessman, Cory decides to sell bobbleheads of the President to the people of Washington DC – but trouble is afoot. See, an evil toymaker has turned the bobbleheads into hypnotic devices, and it’s your job to foil their malign scheme. Ridiculous? Absolutely. But I came into this experience with an open heart and an open mind.

I wasn't convinced by Elden Ring Tarnished Edition until I played it on Nintendo Switch 2 Final Fantasy Resonance review: classic RPG greatness made for 2026 Tales of Eternia Remastered review: a real blast from the past However, as soon as I got into the game, I was instantly struck by frankly horrifying visuals. No, really, I have a feeling Cory’s face will be haunting my nightmares for the foreseeable future. See, characters are so unrefined and blurred that you can’t even see their eyes or expressions. And that’s not inherent to the console – plenty of DS games pulled off nice-looking character models in spite of the handheld’s technical limitations.

Anyway, that’s not the end of the world, at least the gameplay could still be fun! Right? Well, I suppose in a sense, Cory in the House truly is a genre-defining title; in that it defines exactly how not to make an adventure stealth game. Movement is janky, throwing exploding fictional pastries is, somehow, totally mind-numbing, and the various settings are unbelievably bland. You play the occasional mini-game to progress the story, but even these are so laughably basic that I can’t even imagine a child having fun.

Oh, and one more thing. You have a lot of conversations with characters like Cory’s father, bandmates, and store workers – many of which are intended to be funny…at least I think they are? Sometimes I was unsure whether Cory was trying to crack a joke, but luckily, a laugh track would play when it was time for me to giggle. Artificial laughs even seem to play when characters don’t say anything remotely funny, which in itself was actually kinda entertaining. So, I guess there’s that?

So, there you have it, folks. Cory in the House for the Nintendo DS is – in spite of its 9.3 user score on Metacritic – a pretty terrible TV show tie-in, and it’s no wonder that its two critic review scores are listed as a 30 and a 40. Ouch.

Still, I’ve been finding the explosion of ironic meme-fuelled positive reviews pretty funny, even as a massive lover of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 . And while we’re here, it only seems right to recommend this actual masterpiece to anyone who hasn’t tried it yet.

After parting ways with Xbox, I pray that Double Fine is working on more games like Psychonauts 2 — one of the best platformers since Super Mario Odyssey Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave review: the best game on Nintendo Switch 2 so far Resident Evil 2 for Nintendo Switch 2 review: survival horror mastery on the go Yes, Expedition 33 is a phenomenal RPG, with one of the best stories that’s ever been told through the video game medium, in my view. It plates up incredibly addictive gameplay, with an excellent parrying mechanic that’s a joy to master. Combine that with a jaw-droppingly gorgeous visual style and generational soundtrack, and it’s simply a must-play.

No matter how good it is, though, it may not be able to stop the immovable force that is Cory in the House for the Nintendo DS, which, in its own ‘special’ way, is a game that I won’t be forgetting in a hurry.

items.title: 'Clair Obscur: Expedition 33' stripped of Indie Game Awards due to generative AI use
items.summary: It had previously been announced Game of the Year.
items.content:
The Indie Game Awards has stripped Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 of both its Game of the Year and Debut Game awards, citing the roleplaying game's use of generative AI.

Run by Six One Indie , the annual Indie Game Awards aims to highlight excellence in independent video game development. Titles are eligible for consideration in the Indie Game Awards if their developers are outside the "traditional publisher system," and were not owned or financially controlled by a major corporation. Said games also must not have used any generative AI in their development process, which would make them "strictly ineligible for nomination."

Unfortunately, it appears that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 's developer Sandfall Interactive did indeed use generative AI, disqualifying them from the Indie Game Awards.

"The Indie Game Awards have a hard stance on the use of gen AI throughout the nomination process and during the ceremony itself," the Indie Game Awards wrote, announcing its decision over the weekend. "When it was submitted for consideration, a representative of Sandfall Interactive agreed that no gen AI was used in the development of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 .

"In light of Sandfall Interactive confirming the use of gen AI art in production on the day of the Indie Game Awards 2025 premiere, this does disqualify Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 from its nomination. While the assets in question were patched out and it is a wonderful game, it does go against the regulations we have in place."

The Indie Game Awards' Game of the Year and Debut Game will now be awarded to the second-highest scoring titles in each respective category. As such, Debut Game goes to à la mode games ' survival horror Sorry We’re Closed , while the Indie Game Awards' Game of the Year 2025 is Dogubomb 's puzzle adventure game Blue Prince .

The IGAs Nomination Committee is officially retracting Debut Game and Game of the Year, awarding both categories to new recipients. Additionally, we are retracting one of the Indie Vanguard recipients. Full details can be found in our FAQ under Game Eligibility: www.indiegameawards.gg/faq [image or embed]

Sandfall Interactive had previously disclosed its use of AI in a July interview with Spanish newspaper El País , though did not explicitly confirm that the tools they used were generative in nature. At the time, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 's producer François Meurisse merely stated that they had used "some AI" in the game's production. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

In a later update to El País ' article, Sandfall Interactive claimed that no generative AI assets currently remain in Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 . However, it confirmed that generative AI was used to create placeholder textures during development, not all of which were removed prior to release due to oversights in the quality assurance process. Sandfall Interactive states that such AI-generated textures were replaced within five days of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 's launch, and were never intended to be included in the final game.

Players did indeed spot AI-generated textures in Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 upon its April 24 release, quickly calling out suspicious in-game posters on social media . Less than a week later, patch notes for a hotfix noted that the developers had "replaced a placeholder texture with the correct visual asset."

Even so, the Indie Game Awards were apparently unaware of these events, as it did not discover Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 's AI use until Dec. 18, the day the winners were announced.

Reaction to Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 's disqualification from the Indie Game Awards has been mixed. While some fans appreciate the awards' strict stance against generative AI, others feel that Sandfall Interactive's use of the technology to create a few placeholder poster assets was relatively minor and should be permissible in this case. Still, the Indie Game Awards' criteria requires that no generative AI be used at all, regardless of the extent of such use.

"Thank you for standing up and speaking out for a more ethical games industry," wrote @erin-hallow on Bluesky. "In a time where authentic human creativity is under threat and big players perpetuate that issue, it means a lot to see an awards show that truly cares about the authenticity of the games it showcases."

"Considering a single placeholder asset made it into the final version, entirely by mistake, it seems a bit silly but rules are rules I guess," Redditor u/Caridor wrote on the r/expedition33 subreddit . (Note: Technically at least two placeholder assets were spotted, but their sentiment stands. )

items.title: Hotfix 1.5.1 is live!
items.summary: Bug Fixes & Improvements Expeditioners, the 1.5.1 hotfix is now live! Thanks to your reports, we have worked on a number of fixes listed below: Gameplay Fixed Monoco’s weapon “Cannaro” being unobtainable from Chromatic Machinapieds Players
items.content:
Bug Fixes & Improvements

Expeditioners, the 1.5.1 hotfix is now live!

Thanks to your reports, we have worked on a number of fixes listed below:

Gameplay

  • Fixed Monoco’s weapon “Cannaro” being unobtainable from Chromatic Machinapieds

    • Players who already defeated the boss will automatically receive the weapon in their inventory, unless they started a NG+(+) after that

      [/*]
    [/*]

  • Fixed Esquim not applying Mark to all enemies when a skill had 0 hits.

    [/*]

  • Fixed a targeting issue caused by using a Recoat item followed by ‘Retry Battle’, which resulted in the player being unable to target the middle enemy or character.

    [/*]

  • Fixed a soft-lock when attempting to load a save without hovering any slot while backup saves were displayed.

    [/*]

  • Fixed upgrade of the weapons to level 34 when spamming Upgrade weapon and change character buttons

    • Level 34 weapons have been reverted back to level 33

      [/*]
    [/*]

  • Fixed character being able to use other characters' weapon when quickly switching weapon tabs after changing weapon

    [/*]

Environment

  • Nerfed the hardest boss in Verso’s Drafts (red lifebuoy) by moving it slightly to make a quest easier.

    [/*]

  • Fixed various environment issues (collisions, misplaced assets, missing or incorrect footsteps SFX) across Verso's Drafts, the World Map, and other levels.

    [/*]

Audio & Music

  • Improved environmental ambiances and spatial audio for better immersion in Verso’s Drafts

    [/*]

  • Enhanced audio mixes for select characters, combos, and finishers

    [/*]

  • Multiple audio & music issues were resolved, including:

    • Missing music after defeating new Endless Tower bosses.

      [/*]

    • Missing subtitle line for Sciel in one of the new cinematics.

      [/*]

    • Missing Barbapapa status effect SFX when receiving a second stack.

      [/*]

    • Missing some SFX for Licorne enemy in Verso’s Drafts.

      [/*]

    • Missing SFX for Paint Cage explosions in Verso's Drafts.

      [/*]

    • Music and SFX not pausing when opening pause menu during cinematic sequence with slow motion enabled, resulting in audio desynchronization for the remainder of the cinematic sequence

      [/*]
    [/*]

Localization

Fixed various localization issues, including:

  • Subtitles in Root Of All Evil cinematics disappearing too fast.

    [/*]

  • Overlapping text in Pictos & Luminas lists.

    [/*]

  • Autoplay dialogue options swapped when the title is set to LATAM Spanish.

    [/*]

  • Incorrect text displayed during Flying Manor side quest when the title is set to Vietnamese.

    [/*]

  • Verso’s skill Phantom Stars displaying HTML in combat when the title is set to Vietnamese.

    [/*]

Other

We are aware of various issues encountered, particularly the one reported by some of you who are having difficulty launching the title on Windows 11.

One of these issues is caused by Windows Security reporting false positives when launching. This has been fixed as part of the v1.5.1 hotfix as of 17:00 CET.

The other issue causing this problem is related to the Windows Smart App Control feature. Turning it off to fix it is not recommended as this will remove the feature permanently from your system. We are investigating this issue and hope to resolve it as soon as possible so we suggest waiting for the next hotfix!

Until then, 

Tomorrow comes!

And as always thanks for your support and for your reports via the official Typeform!

~ The Expedition 33 Team 

Update 08/01

We've pushed a fix for the soft lock occurring when Braseleur hits the player with orbs during two consecutive enemy turns.
